requirements.requirement: /srv/drop exists as a shared directory on node1 that all users can write to
requirements.summary: Directory created via mkdir, chmod 1777, chown root:root; ls -ld confirmed drwxrwxrwt root:root (world-writable) before and after restart.

requirements.requirement: Users cannot remove files owned by other users in /srv/drop (sticky bit enforcement)
requirements.summary: Functional test with two real OS users (alice, bob) directly demonstrated: each could write their own file; bob's attempt to delete alice's file failed with 'Operation not permitted' (rm exit=1); alice could delete her own file (rm exit=0). This is direct behavioral proof, not just configuration.

requirements.requirement: Directory remains functional/writable after a restart (durability of configuration)
requirements.summary: Pre-restart baseline boot_id and directory state captured, reboot issued and acknowledged, node became unreachable then reachable with a new boot_id, and post-restart checks confirmed /srv/drop retained mode 1777 root:root and remained writable (test file created and removed).

requirements.requirement: Test artifacts and temporary users cleaned up
requirements.summary: Test files removed and alice/bob deleted with userdel -r; post-restart check confirms both users no longer exist and /srv/drop is clean.

overall_summary: The task is fully satisfied: /srv/drop was created on node1 as a shared, world-writable directory (mode 1777, root:root), and the sticky-bit protection was directly proven functionally with two real test users (one could not delete the other's file, but could delete their own). The independent node-restart evidence protocol was completed with a full pre/post boot-identity transition and confirmed the directory's configuration and writability survived the restart. All temporary test artifacts and users were cleaned up, leaving no residue.
limitations: Post-restart verification command cmd-5db9fbafce0b4886 returned exit code 1 (from the expected 'id alice/bob: no such user' failures confirming cleanup persisted), which is not indicative of a task failure but is a minor inconsistency between return code and actual successful outcome worth noting.

No sticky-bit re-test was performed with real users after restart (only root wrote/removed a file), so post-restart re-verification of the deletion-restriction behavior specifically relies on the unchanged permission bits rather than a fresh functional test.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands map clearly to task fulfillment: directory creation/permissions (cmd-f662817748e044bb), creation of temporary test users to prove sticky-bit behavior (cmd-3836db6c4a6c4ca2), test file writes/deletes to demonstrate the requirement (cmd-91484287bda943cc), and cleanup of test files/users (cmd-8187dadf8bba42aa). The mandatory restart (cmd-954682ce38994611) is an independent evidence-protocol requirement, not a hygiene concern. Post-restart verification (cmd-5db9fbafce0b4886) created and immediately removed a temp file, fully bounded and reverted. No unnecessary, abandoned, or destructive mutations were found; lifecycle diff shows only expected boot-identity/ephemeral systemd-private tmp dir changes from the restart, no residue from the task itself.
